sections.heading: DSM-5-TR Organization
sections.content:
The DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022) is organized into three sections:

Section | Content
Section I | Introduction, use of the manual, cautionary statement
Section II | Diagnostic criteria and codes — the 20 major diagnostic chapters
Section III | Emerging measures, cultural formulation, Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD), conditions for further study

Chapter ordering follows a developmental lifespan sequence:

Neurodevelopmental Disorders (ASD, ADHD, ID, LD, Tics)
Schizophrenia Spectrum & Other Psychotic Disorders
Bipolar and Related Disorders
Depressive Disorders
Anxiety Disorders
Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
Dissociative Disorders
Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders
Feeding and Eating Disorders
Elimination Disorders
Sleep-Wake Disorders
Sexual Dysfunctions
Gender Dysphoria
Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders
Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders
Neurocognitive Disorders (Delirium, Major/Mild NCD)
Personality Disorders
Paraphilic Disorders
Other Conditions That May Be a Focus of Clinical Attention (Z-codes)

Key changes from DSM-IV-TR to DSM-5/DSM-5-TR:

Multiaxial system eliminated — no more Axes I-V; all disorders listed together
Uses ICD-10-CM codes for billing and data collection
Personality disorders and medical conditions are now listed alongside other disorders (not separate axes)
DSM-5-TR (2022) updated descriptive text, added prolonged grief disorder, added or revised selected categories and codes, and extensively updated text; consult current APA update supplements because DSM-5-TR receives post-publication changes

sections.heading: Specifiers, Severity, and Course
sections.content:
DSM-5-TR diagnoses are refined using specifiers that provide additional clinical information:

Severity: Mild, Moderate, Severe (based on criteria count, symptom intensity, or functional impairment)
Course: First episode, recurrent, in partial remission, in full remission
Descriptive features: "With anxious distress," "with mixed features," "with psychotic features," "with peripartum onset," "with seasonal pattern"

Example for Major Depressive Disorder:

F32.1 Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, moderate, with anxious distress

EPPP Tip: Specifiers communicate clinically relevant features but do not prescribe treatment by themselves. Treatment planning also requires severity, safety, course, differential diagnosis, medical factors, evidence, preferences, access, and monitoring.

sections.heading: Z-Codes: Other Conditions That May Be a Focus of Clinical Attention
sections.content:
Z-codes (formerly V-codes in DSM-IV) are used for conditions that are not mental disorders but may affect diagnosis, treatment, or prognosis.

Key categories:

Relational problems: Relationship distress with spouse/partner, parent-child relational problem, sibling relational problem
Abuse and neglect: Maltreatment, neglect, and related encounter/context codes require current ICD-10-CM coding guidance; do not assume every such condition is a Z-code or a trauma-disorder diagnosis
Educational and occupational problems: Academic problems, job dissatisfaction
Housing and economic problems: Homelessness, financial problems
Social environment: Social exclusion, target of discrimination
Nonadherence to medical treatment
Malingering: Z76.5 — Not a mental disorder; a condition warranting clinical attention

EPPP Tip: Factors influencing health status or contact can be the principal focus even without a mental disorder. Malingering is not a mental disorder, but coding and documentation should follow current ICD-10-CM and setting rules.

sections.heading: Differential Diagnosis
sections.content:
Differential diagnosis is the systematic process of distinguishing between disorders with overlapping symptoms. The EPPP frequently tests this skill.

Parallel, iterative differential diagnosis tasks:

Assess information and response validity when indicated—avoid assuming that inconsistency means intentional deception; factitious disorder and malingering differ in motivation and can coexist with genuine illness
Assess substances and medications—exposure, dose, timing, interactions, intoxication, withdrawal, and persistence outside exposure windows
Assess medical and neurological explanations—urgent onset, altered attention/awareness, vital-sign or neurological change, injury, infection, metabolic disturbance, sleep, pain, and other indicated data
Evaluate mental-disorder hypotheses—criteria, duration, impairment, exclusion rules, development, culture/language, course, and context
Allow co-occurring and interacting conditions—do not force one “primary” explanation when multiple diagnoses or contextual conditions are supported

High-yield differential diagnosis pairs for the EPPP:

This vs. That | Key Distinguisher
MDD vs. Bipolar II | Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, no manic episode, plus the full criteria and exclusion analysis
Schizophrenia vs. Schizoaffective | Schizoaffective has major mood episodes concurrent with psychotic symptoms, plus psychosis WITHOUT mood symptoms for ≥2 weeks
GAD vs. OCD | GAD and OCD differ in phenomenology, functions, associated behaviors, time course, and criteria; real-life content or insight alone does not decide the diagnosis
PTSD vs. Acute Stress Disorder | Duration: ASD = 3 days to 1 month; PTSD = >1 month
Delirium vs. Dementia (Major NCD) | Delirium centers on acute disturbance in attention and awareness with fluctuation and another physiological cause; major NCD is typically more persistent, but onset and fluctuation vary by etiology and can coexist with delirium
Panic Disorder vs. GAD | Panic = sudden, discrete attacks; GAD = chronic, pervasive worry
Anorexia vs. Bulimia | Anorexia nervosa requires significantly low weight and may include binge/purge behavior; bulimia nervosa requires recurrent binge eating and compensatory behavior not occurring exclusively during anorexia—body weight is not otherwise fixed

sections.heading: Categorical vs. Dimensional Models
sections.content:
This is one of the most important conceptual debates in clinical psychology and is increasingly tested on the EPPP.

Feature | Categorical Model | Dimensional Model
Concept | Disorders are distinct categories — you either have it or you don’t | Traits/symptoms exist on a continuum — everyone has some degree
Example | DSM-5-TR Section II: MDD requires 5+ symptoms | PHQ-9 score of 5 vs. 10 vs. 20 = different severity levels
Strengths | Clear communication, treatment protocols, research consistency | Can represent severity and subthreshold variation; effects on stigma, reliability, and utility depend on construct, measure, threshold, and implementation
Limitations | Arbitrary cutoffs, symptom overlap, comorbidity problem | Requires validated measures, interpretable reference points, and decisions about thresholds; practicality varies by setting
Where used | DSM-5-TR Section II (primary diagnoses) | DSM-5-TR Section III (AMPD), ICD-11 Personality Disorders, Level 1/2 Cross-Cutting Symptom Measures

The DSM-5-TR Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) — Section III:

Criterion A: Level of Personality Functioning Scale (LPFS) — rates impairment in Self (identity, self-direction) and Interpersonal (empathy, intimacy) functioning on 5 levels (0 = none to 4 = extreme)
Criterion B: 5 pathological personality trait domains: Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, Psychoticism (with 25 trait facets)
Only 6 specific PDs retained: Antisocial, Avoidant, Borderline, Narcissistic, Obsessive-Compulsive, Schizotypal
Plus a general "Personality Disorder — Trait Specified" category

EPPP Tip: The AMPD is in Section III, meaning it is an official alternative model in the manual’s Emerging Measures and Models section, not the primary Section II categorical personality-disorder system. It is a hybrid categorical-dimensional model, not a fully dimensional replacement. However, the ICD-11 (used internationally) has adopted a fully dimensional approach to PDs. Know both systems.

sections.heading: Cultural Formulation
sections.content:
The DSM-5-TR includes the Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI) in Section III — a 16-question semi-structured interview that helps clinicians understand the cultural context of a patient’s presenting problem.

Four core CFI domains:

Cultural definition of the problem: the person’s description, language, identity, and reference-group perspectives
Cultural perceptions of cause, context, and support: explanatory models, stressors, supports, identity, discrimination, and meanings
Cultural factors affecting self-coping and past help seeking: coping, barriers, resources, prior services, and what was helpful or unhelpful
Cultural factors affecting current help seeking: preferences, concerns, relationship expectations, and services or supports the person wants now

Key terms:

Cultural concepts of distress (DSM-5-TR term): Replaced "culture-bound syndromes." Includes cultural syndromes, cultural idioms of distress, and cultural explanations
Cultural humility: Ongoing self-reflection about one’s own cultural biases; supports ongoing self-reflection and attention to power; it complements, rather than replaces, demonstrable knowledge and skills for the task

EPPP Tip: Use the CFI when cultural context may improve understanding and care—not only when symptoms seem unusual or the person is from a visibly different group. The CFI enhances but does not independently determine diagnosis. Also know that DSM-5-TR uses "cultural concepts of distress" rather than the older term "culture-bound syndromes."

sections.heading: Putting It Together: The Diagnostic Process
sections.content:
Complete diagnostic assessment flow:

Clinical interview matched to referral question, setting, language, population, and decision stakes → presenting problem, history, psychosocial context
Mental Status Exam → current functioning snapshot
Psychological testing (if indicated) → cognitive, personality, or neurocognitive measures
Cultural formulation → context for understanding symptoms
Differential diagnosis → iterative comparison of medical, substance/medication, developmental, cultural/contextual, response-validity, and mental-disorder hypotheses
Diagnosis + specifiers → ICD-10-CM coded
Case conceptualization → integrates all data into a coherent formulation guiding treatment

EPPP Tip: The diagnostic process is hypothesis-driven. You generate hypotheses from the interview, test them with additional data (tests, records, collateral), and revise as evidence arrives, retain uncertainty where warranted, and allow multiple interacting explanations rather than forcing parsimony. This is the scientist-practitioner model applied to diagnosis.

reflectiveCoda.teaser: Where can AI assist specialized assessment—and where must human legal and clinical judgment remain?
reflectiveCoda.content:
AI may help organize records, draft interview prompts, summarize score patterns, or improve access to educational explanations. Those uses require validated workflows, privacy and security controls, bias monitoring, transparent provenance, and qualified review.

AI must not be treated as the legal decision maker for competency or insanity, a stand-alone predictor of violence, a method for inferring a brain lesion from one score, or an autism diagnostic authority. These judgments depend on jurisdiction, referral context, standardized administration, direct examination, collateral evidence, functional impact, differential hypotheses, and professional accountability.

A useful safeguard is assist, verify, integrate: let a tool assist with bounded tasks; verify its output against source data and standards; and let an accountable professional integrate evidence and communicate uncertainty.
reflectiveCoda.studyNote: 💡 Study Note: (1) Competency = present abilities; insanity = past mental state under jurisdiction-specific law. (2) Neuropsychological tests sample constructs; one score rarely localizes or diagnoses. (3) Pediatric rating scales require cross-source integration. (4) ASD screeners and structured tools support—not replace—comprehensive clinical evaluation.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the Dusky competence-to-stand-trial standard and the limit of that standard?
choices: It concerns the defendant's sufficient present ability to consult with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding and a rational as well as factual understanding of the proceedings; the court applies the legal standard under governing law
It asks whether the defendant knew right from wrong when the alleged offense occurred, making it the same inquiry as criminal responsibility
It is satisfied whenever no severe mental disorder is diagnosed, because diagnosis determines legal competence
It requires perfect recall of the alleged offense and the ability to conduct a defense without assistance from counsel
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Dusky frames competence as a present functional legal capacity: sufficient present ability to consult with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding, plus a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings. It is not the retrospective criminal-responsibility or insanity inquiry, does not require perfect memory, and is not decided solely by the presence or absence of a diagnosis. Clinical assessment can inform the question, but the court makes the legal determination under the applicable jurisdiction's procedures. Competence to stand trial also should not be assumed to answer every other legal-capacity question.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A toddler has an elevated M-CHAT-R/F result and later exceeds an ADOS-2 classification threshold. What is the best next conclusion?
choices: ASD is confirmed because two instruments agree.
The child should wait six months before any referral so false positives can resolve.

A qualified clinician should integrate developmental and caregiver history, direct observation, language/cognitive/adaptive and sensory functioning, impairment, and differential diagnoses while connecting the child with indicated services.
The ADOS-2 result should replace caregiver and school information.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: The best answer treats both instruments as evidence rather than as a self-executing diagnosis. CDC guidance states that no single tool should determine diagnosis; a qualified clinician integrates developmental and caregiver history, direct observation, functioning, diagnostic criteria, impairment, and plausible alternatives. A positive screen or concerning findings warrant timely comprehensive evaluation, and referral for indicated supports does not need to wait for a final diagnostic label.

sections.heading: Forensic Assessment: Competency vs. Insanity
sections.content:
Competency to stand trial and an insanity defense answer different legal questions at different times. Psychological evaluation informs—but does not itself decide—either legal determination.

Feature | Competency to Stand Trial (CST) | Insanity Defense (NGRI)
Timeframe | Present: abilities during the proceedings | Past: mental state at the alleged act
Legal question | Under Dusky, does the defendant have sufficient present ability to consult with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding and a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings? Statutes add jurisdiction-specific detail. | Did a qualifying mental condition meet the jurisdiction's insanity rule at the time of the act? M'Naghten, Model Penal Code, and the federal rule differ; not every jurisdiction recognizes the defense.
Who decides? | The evaluator supplies relevant data and an opinion within the referral and jurisdiction; the court makes the legal determination. | The evaluator addresses the jurisdiction's legal criteria; the judge or fact finder determines the legal outcome.
What follows? | Proceedings generally pause if the defendant is incompetent. Restoration, treatment, review, and disposition depend on governing law and due-process limits; medication is not automatic. | An NGRI verdict can lead to jurisdiction-specific commitment, review, conditional release, or supervision. It does not imply a single automatic placement.

EPPP Tip: Competency is about present adjudicative abilities; insanity is about past mental state under a particular jurisdiction's rule.

sections.heading: Forensic Assessment: Malingering and Risk
sections.content:
In forensic assessment, psychologists may evaluate response validity or violence risk when the referral, competence, and jurisdiction permit. These are probabilistic assessments—not lie detectors or guarantees.

Response and performance validity:

SIRS-2: A structured interview that samples response styles associated with feigned psychiatric symptoms. No single result proves malingering; interpretation integrates records, behavior, collateral information, and alternative explanations.
M-FAST: A brief screen for possible feigned psychiatric symptoms; an elevated result calls for more comprehensive evaluation.
TOMM: A performance-validity measure focused on effort and response validity in memory testing; it is not by itself a diagnosis of malingering.
MMPI validity scales: Patterns can raise hypotheses about overreporting, underreporting, inconsistency, or unusual responding. They require scale-specific norms, context, and converging evidence rather than a simple high/low formula.

Violence risk formulation:

HCR-20 V3: A structured professional judgment guide organizing historical, clinical, and risk-management information to support formulation, scenarios, and management planning. It does not produce certainty about an individual's future behavior.
PCL-R: A clinician-rated measure of psychopathic traits. It may contribute information relevant to some risk formulations but is not a stand-alone violence-risk decision rule.

EPPP Tip: Structured methods improve transparency and consistency, but conclusions still require qualified judgment, multiple data sources, documented limitations, and attention to base rates and consequences.

sections.heading: Neuropsychological Batteries: Fixed vs. Flexible
sections.content:
Neuropsychological assessment evaluates brain-behavior relationships using referral-focused history, observation, tests, validity evidence, and contextual data.

Approach | More standardized / comprehensive | More flexible / hypothesis driven
Selection | A relatively consistent core of measures supports broad coverage and profile comparison. | Measures are selected and adapted to the referral, history, emerging findings, and practical constraints.
Tradeoff | Broad sampling may take longer and include low-yield measures. | Efficient targeting may miss an unanticipated weakness if the initial hypotheses are too narrow.
Examples | Historically, Halstead-Reitan and Luria-Nebraska batteries. | The Boston Process Approach emphasizes how a person solves tasks and analyzes errors; contemporary practice often blends standardized cores with flexible additions.

Administration time is not a defining constant: it varies with the referral, version, patient, accommodations, and measures used. Battery scores describe performance under particular conditions; they do not independently identify lesion location or cause.

expandableCase.title: The Unshifting Patient
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A 55-year-old patient who recently suffered a traumatic brain injury is administered the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST). The examiner changes the sorting rule from "Color" to "Shape," and indicates that the patient's next card placement is "Incorrect." The patient becomes frustrated but continues to place the next 10 cards according to the old "Color" rule.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Perseverative responding and difficulty shifting set
expandableCase.explanation: Continuing the old rule despite corrective feedback is perseverative responding and suggests difficulty shifting cognitive set. WCST performance can be affected by several executive and nonexecutive factors; one result cannot establish a prefrontal lesion or identify the cause of impairment.

sections.heading: Pediatric Assessment: Behavior and Emotions
sections.content:
Pediatric assessment often integrates multiple informants and settings. Differences among parent, teacher, and youth reports are clinically meaningful data—not automatically measurement error. Rating scales support hypotheses and track functioning; they do not diagnose by themselves.

Broad-band measures: BASC and ASEBA forms such as the CBCL sample internalizing, externalizing, adaptive, and other domains across available informants.

Focused measures: Current validated Conners forms and Vanderbilt scales can contribute information about ADHD symptoms and impairment. Selection depends on age, setting, norms, purpose, and local practice; diagnosis also requires history, cross-setting impairment, differential assessment, and other relevant evidence.

EPPP Tip: Choose a broad-band measure for a broad referral and a focused scale for a focused hypothesis—but always integrate multiple methods and sources.

sections.heading: Pediatric Assessment: Autism Spectrum Disorder
sections.content:
ASD evaluation separates screening from diagnosis. A positive screen indicates the need for timely diagnostic evaluation and supports; it does not confirm ASD.

Instrument | Role | Responsible interpretation
M-CHAT-R/F | Parent-report screener validated for toddlers 16–30 months; autism-specific screening is recommended at 18 and 24 months and whenever concern arises. | Follow the scoring and follow-up algorithm. Elevated likelihood prompts referral; it is not a diagnosis.
CARS-2 | Structured rating based on observation and history. | Supports clinical application of diagnostic criteria; no single observation tool fits every setting.
ADOS-2 | Standardized observation of social communication and restricted/repetitive behavior. | Requires appropriate training and is interpreted with developmental history, functioning, and other data—not as a stand-alone confirmation.
ADI-R | Structured caregiver interview about developmental history and behavior. | Can contribute detailed historical evidence but does not replace direct observation or broader evaluation.

Integration map: developmental and medical history + caregiver and school information + direct observation + language, cognitive, adaptive, sensory, and functional assessment + differential diagnosis → clinical application of diagnostic criteria and an individualized support plan.

EPPP Tip: Remember the role, not a “magic pair”: screeners flag risk; structured tools organize evidence; qualified clinicians integrate the complete record.

reflectiveCoda.teaser: A contemporary extension: using AI without outsourcing ethical responsibility
reflectiveCoda.content:
Reflective extension (not a new APA Standard): When psychologists use AI, the psychologist—not the tool—remains responsible for professional judgment. Existing duties concerning competence, informed consent, confidentiality, discrimination, accuracy, delegation, records, and avoiding harm still require attention.

An ethics review should ask what data enter the system, who can access or retain them, whether the tool is valid for the intended population and purpose, how errors and bias will be detected, whether the recipient understands the tool’s role, and whether a qualified human can meaningfully review and override its output.

The current APA Ethics Code does not establish AI as a psychologist or moral agent. Speculation about machine intentions or rights should be separated from the practical, exam-relevant question: how a psychologist applies existing Principles and Standards when selecting, supervising, and communicating about technology.
reflectiveCoda.studyNote: 💡 Study Note: (1) General Principles are aspirational; Ethical Standards are enforceable through APA processes. (2) Current-client sexual relationships are prohibited; former-client relationships remain heavily restricted after two years. (3) A subpoena requires a timely legal response but is not automatic authorization to disclose. (4) Standards 1.04 and 1.05 are conditional—not an “always confront first” rule. (5) Apply jurisdiction-specific reporting and protective-duty law.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Dr. Smith, a clinical psychologist in a small rural town, discovers that the only mechanic in town who can fix her car is also the father of her current 12-year-old therapy client. According to the APA Ethics Code, what is the most appropriate course of action?
choices: Terminate therapy with the child immediately before having the car repaired.
Have the car repaired because agreeing not to discuss the child eliminates every possible boundary risk.

Consider using the mechanic only after assessing whether the limited business contact is reasonably expected to impair objectivity, competence, or effectiveness or risk exploitation or harm, and manage foreseeable boundaries.
Refuse to have the car repaired by him in every circumstance because any business contact is automatically unethical.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Standard 3.05 does not make every overlapping role unethical and does not use ?unavoidable? as a complete safe harbor. The psychologist should assess prospectively whether this limited business contact could reasonably impair objectivity, competence, or effectiveness or create exploitation or harm, while considering the child, caregiver, local alternatives, confidentiality, power, and foreseeable future contact. If the risks are acceptably low, the transaction may be permissible with thoughtful boundary management; if material risks emerge, the psychologist should seek another arrangement. A promise not to discuss therapy does not eliminate every risk.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A psychologist learns during a protected peer-review process that another psychologist may have committed a substantial ethics violation, but the review information cannot be disclosed outside that process. Under APA Ethics Code Standards 1.04 and 1.05, what is the best initial conclusion?
choices: Standard 1.04 requires direct informal confrontation before any other analysis, so the peer-review protection must yield
Standard 1.05 requires an immediate licensing-board report because a substantial allegation is enough to establish reportable harm

The psychologist should determine whether the Code's confidentiality and protected-review exceptions mean those Standards do not require action based on that information, while separately considering authorized safety or legal duties
The protected-review exception establishes that no action may ever be considered, even if independently obtained and lawfully usable information later emerges
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Standards 1.04 and 1.05 do not create an automatic confront-or-report sequence. Each says action is not required when intervention would violate confidentiality rights, and the formal-reporting provision also addresses information obtained while reviewing another psychologist's work when retention of or access to that information is protected. The first task is therefore to identify the source and protection of the information and the scope of the Code provision, not to treat an allegation as an adjudicated fact. The exception is not blanket immunity: independently obtained information and separately applicable, lawfully authorized safety or legal duties require their own analysis, including jurisdiction and consultation where appropriate.

sections.heading: Why This Chapter Matters
sections.content: Ethical, legal, and professional issues are an established EPPP content domain; the exact blueprint emphasis and items vary by exam form and current ASPPB specifications. More importantly, ethics forms the backbone of professional identity in psychology. You must know the five General Principles, the distinction between aspirational versus enforceable standards, and how to apply ethics decision-making models to realistic clinical scenarios. This chapter covers the currently operative 2002 APA Ethics Code with amendments effective in 2010 and 2017; APA has circulated a proposed revision, but a draft is not the governing code.

sections.heading: Structure of the APA Ethics Code
sections.content:
The 2017 APA Ethics Code has four components:

Introduction & Applicability: Explains scope, intent, and application to APA members and student affiliates when activities are part of their scientific, educational, or professional roles
Preamble: States the mission of psychology
General Principles (A–E): Aspirational goals — they guide psychologists toward the highest ideals but are not enforceable
Ethical Standards (1–10): Enforceable rules of conduct — the Standards provide a basis for APA ethics enforcement; licensing-board, institutional, civil, and criminal processes are separate

If an EPPP question asks which part of the code is enforceable, the Ethical Standards—not the Preamble or General Principles—supply enforceable APA rules, while law and licensing rules may impose separate obligations.

sections.heading: The Five General Principles
sections.content:
Memorize these five principles by letter (A–E) and name:

Principle | Name | Core Idea | Key Phrase
A | Beneficence & Nonmaleficence | Strive to benefit those with whom you work; do no harm | "Safeguard the welfare and rights"
B | Fidelity & Responsibility | Establish trust; be aware of professional responsibilities to society and community | "Clarify roles, manage conflicts, accept responsibility, and contribute professional time"
C | Integrity | Promote accuracy, honesty, and truthfulness | "Do not steal, cheat, engage in fraud, or misrepresent"
D | Justice | Fairness and equal access to psychology’s benefits for all persons | "Potential biases, competence limits, and expertise limitations"
E | Respect for People’s Rights and Dignity | Respect privacy, confidentiality, self-determination; recognize cultural differences | "Special safeguards for vulnerable populations"

Mnemonic: "Big Friendly Iguanas Dance Rhythmically" — Beneficence, Fidelity, Integrity, D (Justice), Respect

EPPP Tip: The EPPP loves to test Principle B (Fidelity & Responsibility) because it addresses trust, professional responsibility, conflicts of interest, cooperation, and contributing some professional time for little or no compensation. It does not create a simple mandatory pro-bono quota. Also, Principle E explicitly mentions special safeguards for vulnerable populations.

sections.heading: The Ten Ethical Standards
sections.content:
The enforceable standards are organized into 10 sections. You don’t need to memorize every sub-standard, but you must know the major sections and the high-yield standards within each:

Standard | Title | High-Yield Topics
1 | Resolving Ethical Issues | When ethics code conflicts with law or organizational demands, attempt to resolve. If unresolvable, you may adhere to law/regulations if the code permits.
2 | Competence | Practice within boundaries of competence (2.01); in emergencies, provide needed services outside usual competence only when appropriate services are unavailable and discontinue when the emergency ends or services become available (2.02); refrain when personal problems may impair competence and seek appropriate assistance (2.06)
3 | Human Relations | Avoid unfair discrimination (3.01); avoid sexual harassment (3.02); avoid harmful multiple relationships (3.05); informed consent (3.10)
4 | Privacy & Confidentiality | Maintain confidentiality (4.01); discuss limits of confidentiality at outset (4.02); minimize intrusions on privacy (4.04); disclose only with consent or as permitted by law (4.05)
5 | Advertising & Public Statements | Avoid false/deceptive statements (5.01); do not solicit testimonials from current therapy clients/patients or other people vulnerable to undue influence (5.05)
6 | Record Keeping & Fees | Maintain appropriate records (6.01); fee arrangements at start (6.04); no bartering except when not clinically contraindicated (6.05)
7 | Education & Training | Accurate course descriptions; do not require personal disclosure unless clearly identified in admissions/program materials or needed to evaluate or assist a student whose personal problems may impede competent performance or pose a threat
8 | Research & Publication | IRB approval (8.01); informed consent in research (8.02); deception only when justified and alternatives are unavailable (8.07); debriefing (8.08)
9 | Assessment | Use assessment in valid ways (9.02); informed consent (9.03); provide test data pursuant to a client/patient release, subject to specified harm/misuse limits and law or court-order requirements, while protecting test materials and security (9.04, 9.11); use instruments appropriate for the population (9.06)
10 | Therapy | Informed consent to therapy (10.01); therapy with former sexual partners — at least 2 years must pass (10.08); sexual relationships with current clients — never (10.05)

EPPP Tip: Standard 10.08 is a perennial EPPP favorite: sexual relationships with former therapy clients are prohibited for at least 2 years after termination, and even then are not automatically permissible: the psychologist bears the burden of showing no exploitation in light of all relevant factors and the Code’s exceptional-circumstances standard. Sexual relationships with current clients are always prohibited (10.05).

sections.heading: Multiple Relationships (Standard 3.05)
sections.content:
A multiple relationship occurs when a psychologist is in a professional role with a person AND:

Is also in another role with the same person, OR
Is in a relationship with a person closely associated with the client, OR
Promises to enter into a future relationship with the client

Not all multiple relationships are unethical. The standard says a psychologist must refrain from a multiple relationship if it could reasonably be expected to impair objectivity, competence, or effectiveness, or to risk exploitation or harm.

Key distinctions:

Concept | Definition | Example
Boundary Crossing | A deviation from standard practice that is not harmful and may even be therapeutic | Attending a client’s graduation; self-disclosing relevant personal experience
Boundary Violation | A deviation that is harmful or exploitative | Entering a business partnership with a client; sexual contact

EPPP Tip: The EPPP frequently presents scenarios where a multiple relationship exists but asks whether it is necessarily unethical. The answer depends on whether it could reasonably impair objectivity or cause harm. In rural or small communities, some dual relationships may be unavoidable — the psychologist should document, consult, and take reasonable steps to minimize harm.

sections.heading: Informed Consent (Standard 3.10)
sections.content:
Psychologists obtain informed consent using language reasonably understandable to the person when conducting research or providing assessment, therapy, counseling, or consulting services, except where conducting such activities without consent is mandated by law or governmental regulation or otherwise provided in the Code. Domain-specific Standards add requirements. Informed consent requires:

Capacity: The person is able to understand the information (cognitive ability, age, language)
Information: The person has been given adequate information about the nature of services, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality limits, and the right to withdraw
Voluntariness: The consent is given freely, without coercion

Special situations:

People legally incapable of consent: provide an appropriate explanation, seek assent when feasible, consider preferences and best interests, and obtain permission from a legally authorized person when permitted or required by law (3.10b)
Mandated clients: Inform the client about the nature and limits of services, who will receive the report, and the limits of confidentiality
Court-ordered evaluations: Informed consent may not be required, but the psychologist must inform the individual of the purpose, who requested the evaluation, and the limits of confidentiality

EPPP Tip: Even when a client is mandated (e.g., by a court or employer), the psychologist still has an obligation to inform them about the nature and purpose of the service. Do not describe mandated services as voluntary; explain the anticipated services before proceeding, including whether they are court ordered or otherwise mandated and any limits of confidentiality (3.10c).

sections.heading: Confidentiality & Its Limits (Standard 4)
sections.content:
Confidentiality is a cornerstone of the therapeutic relationship. Standard 4.02 requires psychologists to discuss the relevant limits of confidentiality at the outset of the relationship.

Exceptions to confidentiality (when disclosure is permitted or required):

Exception | Details
Protection from harm | Standard 4.05 permits disclosure without consent where law permits it for a valid protective purpose; governing law, urgency, professional standards, and minimum-necessary reasoning determine the response.
Threat to others | Tarasoff is a California case. Mandatory, permissive, and absent duties vary by jurisdiction; use the applicable statute/case law and reasonable protective options.
Abuse reporting | Child-abuse reporting exists nationwide, while reporter definitions, thresholds, timing, covered persons, and elder/dependent-adult duties vary. Report when the governing law requires it.
Legal process | A subpoena requires a prompt response but is not automatic permission to disclose. Evaluate authorization, privilege, HIPAA, jurisdiction, objections, protective relief, and any judicial order with counsel.
Client consent | Client provides written authorization for release of information
Payment | Standard 4.05 permits minimum-necessary disclosure to obtain payment where law permits; HIPAA pathways and contracts may also apply.

Privilege vs. Confidentiality:

Confidentiality = Ethical & professional obligation to protect client information
Privilege = Legal right that protects client communications from being disclosed in court. Privilege belongs to the client, not the therapist. Jaffee v. Redmond (1996) established federal psychotherapist-patient privilege.

EPPP Tip: A subpoena alone does not require you to release records. You should assert privilege, contact the client, and seek legal counsel. Do not ignore a subpoena and do not automatically disclose. Preserve deadlines, consult appropriately, assert privilege or seek protection where available, and respond only through an authorized legal route and within its scope.

expandableCase.title: The Subpoena Trap
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A psychologist receives a subpoena signed by an attorney representing the ex-husband of a current client in a bitter custody dispute. The subpoena demands the psychologist release the client's entire therapy file by 5:00 PM on Friday.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Preserve the Deadline and Evaluate Privilege
expandableCase.explanation: The psychologist should not ignore the deadline or automatically release the file. The appropriate response depends on validity, jurisdiction, who holds privilege, authorization, HIPAA or other privacy law, and available objections or protective orders. Promptly preserve the records, notify or consult the client when appropriate, obtain legal advice, assert privilege or seek protection where available, and disclose only through a legally authorized route and only within its scope.

sections.heading: Ethical Decision-Making Models
sections.content:
When facing an ethical dilemma, psychologists should use a systematic decision-making process rather than relying on intuition alone.

Common model (Koocher & Keith-Spiegel):

Determine that an ethical issue exists
Consult the APA Ethics Code, relevant laws, and regulations
Consider all relevant factors (client welfare, contextual forces, personal biases)
Consult with colleagues, ethics committees, or legal counsel
Generate alternative courses of action
Evaluate each alternative using ethical principles, consequences, and professional guidelines
Choose the best course of action
Implement the decision and monitor outcomes
Document the process

When the Ethics Code conflicts with law:

Standard 1.02: If there is a conflict between ethics and law, the psychologist must make known the commitment to the Ethics Code and attempt to resolve the conflict in a responsible manner
If the conflict remains unresolvable, the Ethics Code states that psychologists may adhere to requirements of law, regulations, or other governing legal authority, subject to the human-rights limitation
However, under no circumstances does this standard permit the psychologist to justify or defend violating human rights (2010 amendment, a response to psychologists’ involvement in interrogation programs)

EPPP Tip: The 2010 amendment to Standard 1.02 added the human rights clause. This was motivated by the controversies around psychologist involvement in enhanced interrogation. Know the operative rule and human-rights limitation; do not infer that every law-versus-ethics conflict has the same solution.

sections.heading: Resolving Ethical Violations (Standard 1.04 & 1.05)
sections.content:
What to do when you become aware of another psychologist’s ethical violation:

Standard 1.04 (Informal Resolution): If the matter seems appropriate for informal resolution and you believe it can be resolved by bringing it to the attention of the individual, attempt that first — unless doing so would violate confidentiality rights or the violation is not appropriate for informal resolution (e.g., sexual misconduct, serious harm)
Standard 1.05 (Reporting): When an apparent violation has substantially harmed or is likely substantially to harm a person or organization and informal resolution is inappropriate or unsuccessful, take further action appropriate to the situation (e.g., filing a complaint with an ethics board, state licensing board, or institutional authority)

EPPP decision tree for ethics violations:

Does an apparent violation appear to have substantially harmed or be likely to substantially harm someone, and is informal resolution appropriate? → Consider bringing it to the person’s attention (1.04)
If substantial harm is present and informal resolution is inappropriate or unsuccessful → consider further action appropriate to the situation (1.05)
Would action violate confidentiality rights, or does the information come from a protected review/retention process? → Standards 1.04 and 1.05 may not require that action; do not assume reporting is allowed

EPPP Tip: Do not use an “always confront first” shortcut. Apply the substantial-harm threshold, appropriateness of informal resolution, confidentiality and review-process exceptions, and the actions available in the facts.

reflectiveCoda.teaser: A contemporary extension: competence and supervision when psychologists use AI
reflectiveCoda.content:
Reflective extension grounded in current APA guidance: A psychologist who uses AI remains responsible for the professional service. Competence includes understanding a tool’s intended use, evidence, limitations, privacy and security implications, population fit, and the circumstances in which its output needs verification or should not be used.

AI-related work should be delegated and supervised like other consequential work: define the task, ensure that people using the tool are trained, protect confidential data, monitor performance, provide meaningful human review, document material decisions, and discontinue use when misinformation, bias, or unsafe performance cannot be adequately mitigated.

APA’s current AI guidance emphasizes transparency and informed consent, bias mitigation, critical evaluation of output, and human oversight. AI can support judgment; it does not become the accountable supervisor, clinician, or final decision-maker.
reflectiveCoda.studyNote: 💡 Study Note: (1) Standard 2.01 defines competence boundaries; 2.02 is a limited emergency exception. (2) Standard 2.06 focuses on whether personal problems threaten adequate professional performance. (3) Standard 2.05 requires competent delegation and reasonable oversight; civil liability is not automatic. (4) IDM development may vary by domain. (5) Cultural humility and demonstrable competence are complementary.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A supervisor assigns a trainee an assessment the trainee has never administered, provides no training or review, and signs the report without examining the data. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The trainee bears primary responsibility for administration, so the supervisor's ethical duty is limited to confirming that a credentialed trainee signed the report.
The clinic's general disclosure that trainees provide services substantially satisfies the supervisor's delegation duty unless the client objects.

The facts directly raise a Standard 2.05 concern about competent delegation and oversight; any civil liability still depends on governing law and facts such as duty, breach, causation, harm, and agency.
The supervisory relationship is ordinarily sufficient to establish civil liability if the assessment later contributes to an adverse decision, even without a separate causation-and-harm analysis.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: APA Ethics Code Standard 2.05 directs psychologists who delegate work to take reasonable steps to avoid assigning duties to people whose relationships could create exploitation or loss of objectivity, authorize only work the person can be expected to perform competently based on training or experience, and see that delegated work is performed competently. Assigning an unfamiliar assessment without training and signing an unchecked report therefore raises a direct ethical concern. That conclusion does not resolve a civil claim: liability standards, agency rules, available causes of action, duty, breach, causation, legally cognizable harm, defenses, and allocation of responsibility vary by jurisdiction and case facts. General consent neither supplies competence nor erases oversight obligations.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Within the Integrated Developmental Model of supervision, a supervisee is eager to learn but anxious, highly dependent on the supervisor, and focused mainly on personal performance. Which classification and qualification are most accurate?
choices: Level 2, because variable autonomy and a shifting focus toward the client define every highly motivated beginner
Level 1 in the relevant practice domain; the pattern guides developmentally responsive supervision rather than serving as a global diagnosis or fixed rank
Level 3, because strong motivation by itself establishes stable autonomy and integrated client awareness
Level 3i, because dependency on a supervisor is the defining feature of an independently practicing professional
knowledgeChecks.rationale: In the IDM, Level 1 is characterized by substantial self-focus, relatively high and partly extrinsic motivation often accompanied by anxiety, and considerable dependence on supervisory structure. Level 2 brings more other-awareness and fluctuation between dependence and autonomy, while Level 3 reflects more stable intrinsic motivation, conditional autonomy, and integrated self-other awareness. Development is domain-specific: the same supervisee can function differently across assessment, intervention, ethics, or other activities. The model supports tailored supervision and reassessment; it is not a diagnosis, licensure decision, or immutable label.

This chapter covers APA Standards 2.01–2.06, major supervision models, and the ethics of delegation.

sections.heading: Boundaries of Competence (Standard 2.01)
sections.content:
Standard 2.01 requires psychologists to provide services only within the boundaries of their competence, based on their:

Education
Training
Supervised experience
Consultation
Study
Professional experience

Working with new populations: When psychologists plan to provide services to new populations (e.g., a different age group, cultural group, or presenting problem), they must obtain relevant training, supervision, consultation, or study to ensure competence.

Emergencies (Standard 2.02): Psychologists may provide services in emergencies to individuals for whom other mental health services are not available, even if they lack the relevant specialized training. However, they must discontinue once the emergency is resolved or appropriate services become available.

EPPP Tip: If a question presents a psychologist who has never worked with children being asked to treat a suicidal child in a rural area with no other providers, the emergency exception may permit limited needed services while alternatives are unavailable; obtain consultation where feasible, work within the emergency need, and discontinue or transfer when the emergency ends or appropriate services become available.

sections.heading: Professional Impairment (Standard 2.06)
sections.content:
Standard 2.06 (Personal Problems and Conflicts) addresses the impaired psychologist:

2.06(a): Psychologists refrain from initiating an activity when they know or should know there is a substantial likelihood that personal problems will prevent competent performance
2.06(b): When psychologists become aware that personal problems may interfere with adequately performing work-related duties, they take appropriate measures, such as obtaining professional consultation or assistance, and determine whether to limit, suspend, or terminate duties

Common sources of impairment:

Substance abuse
Mental health concerns (depression, PTSD, burnout)
Personal crises (divorce, bereavement)
Physical illness or cognitive decline

What to do when a colleague appears impaired:

Apply Standard 1.04 only when an apparent violation has caused or is likely to cause substantial harm and informal resolution appears appropriate; confidentiality and protected-review exceptions matter
When substantial harm is present and informal resolution is inappropriate or unsuccessful, consider further action appropriate to the situation under Standard 1.05; reporting is not automatic or always authorized
Many states have Colleague Assistance Programs (CAPs) that provide confidential support

EPPP Tip: The EPPP tests the distinction between distress (personal suffering that doesn’t affect work) and impairment (personal problems that DO compromise professional functioning). Personal distress is not identical to professional impairment, but psychologists should assess functional impact and foreseeable risk rather than wait for demonstrated harm.

sections.heading: Delegation of Work (Standard 2.05)
sections.content:
Standard 2.05 governs when psychologists delegate work to employees, supervisees, research assistants, or interpreters:

Authorize only those responsibilities the person can reasonably perform competently, based on their training and experience
Ensure the person performs competently
Avoid delegating to persons who have multiple relationships with those being served that could compromise objectivity

Supervisory and vicarious liability: Legal responsibility is fact- and jurisdiction-specific. Respondeat superior can make an employer or principal responsible for acts within an employment or agency scope; supervisors may also face direct liability for negligent selection, delegation, instruction, monitoring, or intervention.

A supervisee, supervisor, employer, or organization may face different theories of liability depending on role, control, conduct, causation, and governing law
Ethically, supervisors authorize only work the delegate can perform competently and take reasonable steps to ensure competent performance
Clear informed consent about trainee involvement, direct observation or other appropriate monitoring, timely feedback, escalation, and accurate documentation support client protection and accountability

EPPP Tip: Do not use an automatic “both are liable” shortcut. Separate the supervisee’s conduct, the supervisor’s own ethical duties, any employment/agency relationship, and the elements of each legal claim.

sections.heading: Supervision Models
sections.content:
These models provide common frameworks for understanding how supervision focus and style can vary:

Model | Developer | Key Concept
Integrated Developmental Model (IDM) | Stoltenberg & Delworth (1987); Stoltenberg & McNeill (2010) | IDM describes developmental levels (1–3i) through patterns in motivation, autonomy, and self-and-other awareness. Level may differ across professional domains or tasks, and supervision is tailored to the current profile rather than a global label.
Discrimination Model | Bernard (1979, 1997) | Supervisor adopts one of three roles (Teacher, Counselor, Consultant) across three foci (process skills, conceptualization skills, personalization skills) = 9 possible combinations.
Competency-Based Supervision | Falender & Shafranske (2004) | Focus on measurable competencies (knowledge, skills, attitudes, meta-competencies). Uses behavioral anchors and direct observation.
Psychotherapy-Based Models | Various | Apply a specific therapy orientation to supervision (e.g., CBT supervision uses Socratic questioning; psychodynamic supervision analyzes parallel process).

IDM Levels in Detail:

Level | Motivation | Autonomy | Awareness | Best Supervision Style
Level 1 | High (eager but anxious) | Low (dependent on supervisor) | Self-focused ("Am I doing this right?") | Structured, didactic, supportive
Level 2 | Fluctuating (confusion, frustration) | Growing but unstable (dependency-autonomy conflict) | Client-focused (becoming more aware of client dynamics) | Less structure; more autonomy; process-oriented
Level 3 | Stable (realistic confidence) | Substantial, with recognized limits (knows when to seek consultation) | Balanced (self AND client) | Consultative, collegial
Level 3i | Integrated across domains | Flexible | Integrative | Peer consultation

EPPP Tip: For the IDM, Know the three structures (motivation, autonomy, awareness) and how they change across levels. A Level 1 supervisee often needs structure and encouragement; a Level 2 benefits from support for the dependency-autonomy conflict; and a Level 3 often benefits from collegial consultation. Apply the profile to the specific domain or task rather than treating it as a global competence verdict.

sections.heading: Parallel Process in Supervision
sections.content:
Parallel process is a psychodynamic concept in which the dynamics of the therapy relationship are unconsciously reenacted in the supervisory relationship (or vice versa).

Examples:

A supervisee whose client feels helpless and dependent may begin to act helpless and dependent with the supervisor
A supervisor who is directive and controlling may find the supervisee becoming directive and controlling with their client
A therapist struggling with a resistant client may present the case with resistance to the supervisor

Clinical use: When recognized, parallel process provides valuable clinical data. The supervisor can say: "I notice you’re asking me to tell you exactly what to do. Is your client doing the same thing with you?" This intervention uses the supervisory relationship as a window into the therapy relationship.

EPPP Tip: If a question describes a supervisee behaving in a way that mirrors their client’s behavior, the answer is parallel process. It can flow in either direction — client → therapist → supervisor, or supervisor → therapist → client.

expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A usually active, engaged psychology intern presents a case to their supervisor in a flat, resistant, and evasive manner, repeatedly stating, "I just don't know what you want me to do." The client being discussed is a severely depressed, passive-aggressive teenager who was mandated to therapy by his parents.

expandableCase.explanation: The intern is unconsciously reenacting the dynamics of the therapy room within the supervision hour. The intern is treating the supervisor the same way the teenage client is treating the intern. Identifying this "parallel process" provides the supervisor with powerful diagnostic information about the relational pull occurring in the actual therapy session.

sections.heading: Cultural Competence in Practice
sections.content:
Standard 2.01(b) requires relevant training, experience, consultation, or supervision when scientific or professional knowledge establishes that identity, cultural, linguistic, disability, socioeconomic, or related factors are essential to effective work. Standard 2.01(c) separately addresses work in emerging areas.

Key concepts:

Cultural responsiveness and competence: context-specific knowledge, skills, attitudes, and reflective practice needed for effective work; competence is maintained and reassessed rather than permanently achieved.
Cultural humility (Tervalon & Murray-García, 1998): An ongoing process of self-reflection, recognizing one’s own biases, and engaging in lifelong learning. Emphasizes the power differential between clinician and client.
Multicultural orientation (Davis et al., 2018): Integrates cultural humility with cultural comfort (therapist’s ease discussing cultural topics) and cultural opportunities (creating space for cultural dialogue in session).

APA Multicultural Guidelines (2017):

Psychologists seek to recognize and understand their own identity development and biases
Psychologists aspire to understand the worldviews and experiences of culturally diverse individuals
Psychologists use culturally appropriate assessment and intervention strategies

EPPP Tip: Avoid treating cultural humility and competence as rivals. Humility supports ongoing self-reflection and attention to power; competence also requires relevant knowledge, skills, consultation, and evaluation for the particular work. If a question asks for the best approach when a psychologist is unfamiliar with a client’s culture, the answer involves seeking consultation, education, and practicing cultural humility — not assuming competence based on a single workshop.

sections.heading: Continuing Education and Maintenance of Competence
sections.content:
Competence is not static. Psychologists have an ongoing obligation to maintain and update their professional knowledge and skills.

Continuing education: renewal periods, hour totals, acceptable formats, and documentation are jurisdiction-specific and change over time
Required topics: some boards mandate ethics, law, cultural responsiveness, suicide prevention, or other subjects; verify the current board rule
Learning method: CE can contribute to maintenance, but reading, consultation, supervised practice, outcome monitoring, and formal training may be needed when expanding competence
Self-assessment: APA encourages psychologists to regularly evaluate their own competence and identify areas for growth

EPPP Tip: If a question asks about maintaining competence over time, consider the actual competence gap and choose education, consultation, supervision, deliberate practice, referral, outcome monitoring, or limits on practice proportionate to the task. Competence is a process, not a one-time achievement.

reflectiveCoda.teaser: A contemporary extension: legal accountability when psychologists use AI tools
reflectiveCoda.content:
Reflective extension (not a settled EPPP rule): AI does not erase a psychologist's existing duties. A psychologist remains responsible for practicing within competence and scope, protecting confidential information, evaluating vendors and data flows, obtaining appropriate consent, checking outputs, and avoiding unsupported clinical conclusions.

Different laws may attach to different actors and data: licensure law governs professional practice; HIPAA may govern covered entities and business associates; consumer-protection, disability, employment, education, product, contract, and negligence law may also apply. Whether a tool is regulated and who may be liable depend on its use, claims, deployment, jurisdiction, and facts.

The practical reasoning sequence is: identify the human decision and foreseeable harm, identify who controls the data and professional judgment, map the applicable legal and ethical duties, preserve meaningful human review, and document why the tool was appropriate. Claims that AI has no legal framework or that one actor is always liable are too broad.
reflectiveCoda.studyNote: 💡 Study Note: (1) Malpractice generally requires duty, breach, harm, and causation. (2) HIPAA psychotherapy notes receive special protection but have limited exceptions. (3) IDEA eligibility is individualized; passing grades do not rule it out. (4) A subpoena requires a prompt legal response but is not automatic permission to disclose. knowledgeChecks.prompt: A psychologist leaves a client's labeled intake folder in a waiting room. Another patient sees the folder but reportedly does not open it before staff retrieve it. The client alleges malpractice. Which conclusion is most defensible from these facts alone?
choices: The lapse warrants ethical, privacy, mitigation, and documentation analysis, but malpractice cannot be decided from the exposure alone; governing law and proof of duty, breach, legally cognizable injury, and causation still matter.
The privacy lapse and a potential regulatory violation are sufficient to establish both breach and damages for a malpractice claim.
No confidentiality or security concern exists unless the psychologist intended another person to read the records.
Because the folder reportedly was not opened, the incident may warrant internal documentation but cannot support a negligence claim or an external response.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Leaving identifiable intake material accessible can raise serious confidentiality, record-security, notification, mitigation, documentation, ethics, licensing, contractual, or regulatory issues even if the exposure was brief and unintended. A professional-negligence claim is a separate legal question. Generally described elements include duty, breach of the applicable standard, causation, and legally cognizable damages, but their definitions, evidentiary rules, available remedies, and related causes of action vary by jurisdiction. The vignette does not establish what information was perceived, what injury occurred, or which law controls, so neither automatic success nor categorical failure follows. The psychologist should protect the record, assess and document the incident, follow applicable law and policy, and obtain qualified legal or risk-management guidance rather than offer the client a guaranteed litigation prediction.

sections.heading: Why This Chapter Matters
sections.content: Psychologists operate within a complex web of federal and state laws that define their scope of practice, mandate certain actions (like reporting abuse), and create legal liability when standards are not met. The EPPP tests your knowledge of licensure requirements, key federal statutes (HIPAA, FERPA, IDEA, ADA), malpractice law, and the duties psychologists owe to clients and third parties. These topics require careful distinction between federal rules, jurisdiction-specific law, ethics, and institutional policy.

sections.heading: Licensure and Scope of Practice
sections.content:
Licensure is the legal authorization to practice psychology independently. It is governed at the state level, not the federal level.

Key facts:

The ASPPB (Association of State and Provincial Psychology Boards) administers the EPPP and facilitates licensure mobility
Jurisdictions set their own education, examination, supervised-experience, and title requirements; doctoral training is commonly required for independent psychologist licensure
Required supervised experience and whether it must occur after the doctorate vary by jurisdiction
Scope of practice defines what a psychologist is legally authorized to do (assessment, therapy, consultation, supervision)
Prescriptive authority is jurisdiction- and credential-specific and changes over time; verify the current psychology board and prescribing law rather than memorizing a fixed state list

Title vs. Practice Acts:

Type | What It Restricts | Example
Title Act | Who can call themselves a psychologist | Only licensed individuals may use the title "psychologist"
Practice Act | Who can perform psychological services | Only licensed individuals may conduct psychological assessment and treatment

EPPP Tip: A practice act is more restrictive than a title act. Licensure authority is jurisdiction-specific. PSYPACT can authorize qualifying telepsychology or temporary in-person practice in participating jurisdictions, but it does not convert one license into a universal license.

sections.heading: Malpractice: The Four Ds
sections.content:
Malpractice commonly refers to professional negligence. Under governing jurisdictional law, a plaintiff generally must prove each required element; the familiar "Four Ds" are a teaching mnemonic for duty, dereliction or breach, damage, and causation:

Element | Definition | Example
Duty | A professional relationship existed, creating a duty of care | The psychologist had a client in therapy
Dereliction (Breach) | The psychologist’s conduct fell below the standard of care | The psychologist failed to assess for suicidality despite clear risk factors
Damage | The client suffered actual harm | The client attempted suicide and was hospitalized
Causation | The breach was a factual and legally sufficient cause of the harm, using the jurisdiction’s applicable actual/proximate-cause rules | The evidence connects the proven breach to the claimed harm under the governing causation standard

Recurring sources of professional liability and discipline include:

Sexual relationships and boundary violations
Breach of confidentiality
Failure to obtain informed consent
Negligent diagnosis or treatment
Failure to take legally required protective action when a serious threat arises

Standard of care = what a reasonably prudent psychologist with similar training and experience would do in the same situation. It is NOT perfection — it is reasonable professional behavior.

EPPP Tip: A professional-negligence claim fails if a required element is not proved under governing law—for example, breach without legally cognizable harm or harm not caused by the breach. That conclusion does not determine whether an ethics complaint, licensing action, contract claim, or another legal theory could proceed.

sections.heading: HIPAA: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
sections.content:
HIPAA (1996) is a federal law that protects the privacy and security of individuals’ Protected Health Information (PHI).

Key provisions for psychologists:

Privacy Rule: Limits who can access PHI and under what circumstances
Security Rule: Requires safeguards (administrative, physical, and technical) for electronic PHI (ePHI)
Minimum Necessary Standard: When it applies, covered entities take reasonable steps to limit PHI to what is needed. Important exceptions include treatment disclosures, disclosures to the individual, authorized disclosures, disclosures required by law, and specified HIPAA compliance uses.
Psychotherapy Notes: HIPAA provides enhanced protection for psychotherapy notes (process notes kept separately from the medical record). Most uses and disclosures require a specific authorization that is not combined with authorization for other PHI, but HIPAA contains limited exceptions, including use by the originator for treatment and disclosures required by law

Psychotherapy notes vs. medical records:

Category | Example | HIPAA Protection
Medical Record | Diagnosis, treatment plan, dates of service, medications, test results | Subject to the applicable Privacy Rule pathway: authorization, permitted use/disclosure, required disclosure, or individual access right
Psychotherapy Notes | Clinician’s private impressions, process notes, analysis of conversation | Special protection; specific authorization is generally required, subject to limited regulatory exceptions

EPPP Tip: HIPAA’s psychotherapy notes provision is heavily tested. Know that these notes are kept separately from the medical record and require their own authorization for release. Do not assume a general authorization covers psychotherapy notes; apply the specific authorization rule and its limited exceptions.

sections.heading: FERPA, IDEA, and ADA
sections.content:
Three federal laws are critical for psychologists working in educational, school, and disability-related settings:

Law | Year | What It Protects/Requires | Key EPPP Facts
FERPA | 1974 | Privacy of student educational records | Rights generally belong to parents and transfer to an eligible student at age 18 or attendance at a postsecondary institution. FERPA permits specified disclosures without consent; education records covered by FERPA are excluded from HIPAA PHI.
IDEA | 1975/2004 | Free Appropriate Public Education (FAPE) for children with disabilities ages 3–21 | Requires an IEP (Individualized Education Program), LRE (Least Restrictive Environment), multidisciplinary evaluation, and due process protections. Discipline rules turn on whether removals constitute a change of placement and on manifestation determinations; IDEA requires or contemplates an FBA/BIP in specified circumstances, not automatically after every suspension exceeding ten days.
ADA | 1990 | Prohibits discrimination against individuals with disabilities in employment, public services, and accommodations | Requires reasonable accommodations unless they cause undue hardship. Covers mental health conditions (depression, anxiety, PTSD, bipolar) if they substantially limit major life activities.

Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (1973): Prohibits disability discrimination in any program receiving federal funding. Section 504 requires an appropriate education and procedural safeguards for eligible students; schools commonly document services and accommodations in a 504 plan, but eligibility and obligations are broader than a form label.

EPPP Tip: IDEA vs. Section 504 is a common EPPP comparison. IDEA eligibility requires a qualifying disability and a need for special education and related services; Section 504 uses its own disability and educational-need standards. Either framework may involve services and accommodations, so determine eligibility individually rather than using an instruction-versus-accommodation shortcut.

sections.heading: Duty to Warn and Protect: Tarasoff and Beyond
sections.content:
Tarasoff is a California decision recognizing a duty to use reasonable care to protect a foreseeable victim under the circumstances presented. Other jurisdictions define mandatory, permissive, or absent duties differently by statute and case law.

The case: Prosenjit Poddar told his therapist at UC Berkeley that he intended to kill Tatiana Tarasoff. The therapist notified campus police but did not warn Tarasoff or her family. Poddar killed Tarasoff. The California Supreme Court ruled that the therapist had a duty to protect.

Two Tarasoff rulings:

Tarasoff I (1974): Established duty to warn — therapist must warn the intended victim
Tarasoff II (1976): Broadened to duty to protect — therapist must take reasonable steps to protect the victim (warning is one option; others include hospitalization, notifying police, modifying treatment)

State variation:

Some states follow duty to warn (must directly warn the intended victim)
Some states follow duty to protect (broader range of protective actions)
Some states have permissive statutes (therapist may warn but is not required to)
Some states have no Tarasoff-type statute at all

Common exam factors (not universal jurisdictional elements):

A serious threat of harm (not vague expressions of anger)
An identifiable or reasonably foreseeable victim or class, where required by the governing law
A therapeutic relationship exists (duty arises from the professional role)

EPPP Tip: The EPPP tests the distinction between Tarasoff I (warn) and Tarasoff II (protect). Know the historical warn/protect distinction, then follow the question's stated jurisdictional rule rather than assuming California law applies everywhere.

sections.heading: Privilege, Subpoenas, and Court Orders
sections.content:
A demand is not automatic permission for unrestricted disclosure. Psychotherapist-patient privilege can protect confidential communications from compelled disclosure, subject to governing jurisdictional law. Critical distinctions:

Concept | Definition | Key Facts
Confidentiality | Ethical and professional obligation | Governed by APA Ethics Code and HIPAA; applies in all contexts
Privilege | Legal right protecting communications in court | Belongs to the client, not the therapist; can be waived by the client

Jaffee v. Redmond (1996): The U.S. Supreme Court established a federal psychotherapist-patient privilege, holding that confidential communications between a licensed psychotherapist and a patient are protected from compelled disclosure in federal proceedings.

Subpoena vs. Court Order:

Subpoena: A formal demand that may be attorney- or court-issued. Do not ignore it or automatically disclose; promptly assess validity, jurisdiction, privilege, authorization, HIPAA, objections, deadlines, and available protective procedures.
Court order: A judicial directive requiring a timely response. Comply as legally required while considering appeal, stay, protective-order, privilege, and scope options with counsel; disclose no more than the order and applicable law require.

What to do when you receive a subpoena:

Do NOT automatically release records
Contact the client and discuss — client may consent or waive privilege
Seek legal consultation
Assert privilege on behalf of the client
If necessary, file a motion to quash the subpoena
Respond through the legally appropriate route; disclosure may rest on authorization, an order, another HIPAA permission or requirement, or other applicable law

EPPP Tip: This is one of the most commonly tested legal questions: a subpoena alone is NOT enough to release records. The psychologist should assert privilege, contact the client, and seek legal counsel. A subpoena requires a timely legal response but does not automatically authorize disclosure; evaluate privilege, HIPAA, applicable law, and protective options.

sections.heading: Mandatory Reporting
sections.content:
All 50 states have mandatory reporting laws for child abuse and neglect. Psychologists are classified as mandated reporters in every state.

Key principles:

Reporting thresholds vary in wording by jurisdiction (for example, reasonable suspicion, reasonable cause, or reasonable belief); proof is generally not required
Failure to report can carry jurisdiction-specific criminal, civil, licensing, or employment consequences
Statutes commonly provide qualified immunity for good-faith reports, with wording and exceptions varying by jurisdiction
You do NOT need client consent to make a report
Reporting obligations override confidentiality

Who is covered:

Child abuse/neglect: Mandatory in all states
Elder abuse: Mandatory in most states
Dependent adult abuse: Mandatory in many states
Domestic violence: Varies by state; generally NOT mandatory for adult victims (except in some states like California)

EPPP Tip: When facts meet the governing reporting threshold, make the required report promptly; do not investigate beyond what is needed to determine the reporting duty. You should inform the client that you are required to file a report, but you file even if the client objects. Use the threshold, reporter category, child definition, timing, agency, and documentation rules supplied by the jurisdiction.

reflectiveCoda.teaser: A contemporary extension: evaluating AI-assisted assessment as an assessment method
reflectiveCoda.content:
Reflective extension grounded in current assessment principles: An AI-generated score, classification, or narrative is not self-validating. The psychologist must identify the construct and intended use, examine reliability and validity evidence for the relevant population and setting, evaluate fairness and accessibility, and understand how model updates or data drift may change performance.

Assessment responsibility also includes informed consent and transparency, privacy and data governance, test security, identity and administration conditions, human review, and a process for correcting errors. An appealing narrative cannot substitute for sufficient data or evidence supporting the interpretation.

APA’s current AI guidance emphasizes critical evaluation, bias mitigation, transparency, and human oversight. The 2014 Testing Standards remain the current edition while a revision is underway; neither source makes every AI tool suitable for psychological assessment.
reflectiveCoda.studyNote: 💡 Study Note: (1) Test data and test materials have different definitions and conditional duties—avoid absolute release/refuse rules. (2) Standard 9.10’s explanation duty has a relationship-based advance-notice exception. (3) Standard 9.08 bars decisions based on obsolete tests or outdated results. (4) Validity concerns interpretations and uses supported by evidence. (5) Automated output requires competent human evaluation.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A client signs a release directing the psychologist to send the client’s raw scores and response data to a named qualified psychologist, and separately asks for a blank test manual and item booklet. What is the best response under Standards 9.04 and 9.11?
choices: Send everything because a signed release overrides test-security duties.
Refuse both requests because all assessment information is protected test material.
Apply the 9.04 release pathway to the requested test data and recipient, while protecting the blank manual and item booklet under 9.11 consistent with law and contractual obligations.
Send only a narrative interpretation because raw scores can never be test data.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: The keyed response keeps Standards 9.04 and 9.11 distinct. Test data can include raw and scaled scores and the client?s responses, and a valid release to a named qualified psychologist ordinarily triggers the 9.04 pathway subject to its exceptions and applicable law. A blank manual and unused item booklet are test materials whose security remains protected consistent with law, publisher contracts, and professional obligations. A release is not a waiver of every security duty, but neither is test security a categorical reason to withhold all client test data or provide only a narrative summary.

This chapter also covers the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014), a leading consensus source for responsible test development, evaluation, and use; it is guidance rather than a substitute for law, regulation, the Ethics Code, or test-specific evidence.
